title: Site Heat Scorecard
one_liner: Score candidate data center sites for local political and permitting risk, then export a one-page memo.
speaker: Salim Ismail
context: Salim says opposition to big tech and data centers shaped the midterms, Goldman estimates 45% of planned US build could face restrictions, and candidates calling for pauses won governor races. Dave adds that building will move to friendly states.
demo: A developer enters candidate sites with simple facts: state, county, whether a moratorium is proposed or passed, the next vote date, distance to homes, water source, any tax abatement, and known opposition groups. The tool gives each site a weighted 0–100 risk score with the reasons spelled out, ranks the sites, and builds a printable memo. With a pasted API key it can also draft talking points for the community; without one, an example mode fills these in and labels them as examples.
data_plan: The customer's own inputs. Default risk weights are editable and labelled as the tool's assumptions. Episode figures (56% opposition, 45% of planned build at risk, 12 governor races) appear only as context.
risks: Collecting county agendas is messy and some sites block scraping. Big developers may already pay lobbyists and consultants for this. The topic could cool off if the politics change.

opportunity.title: Moratorium Radar
opportunity.one_liner: A weekly briefing that tracks county and state data center moratoriums, zoning votes and opposition for site developers.
opportunity.customer: Mid-size data center developers, powered-land brokers, site-selection consultants and landowners trying to sell land for data centers in the US
opportunity.problem: Projects that are planned but not yet zoned can be killed by a local moratorium or a hostile county board. Today, tracking hundreds of county agendas, ordinances and opposition groups is done by hand or not at all.
opportunity.revenue_model: Subscription, about $300–$1,000 a month per firm for weekly state and county briefings, plus one-off site risk memos at about $1,500 each (estimate)
opportunity.why_now: The election made data centers a political issue in both parties. The hosts say the market priced in slowdowns for projects that are planned but not yet approved, and that building will move to states that welcome it.
